discovery: Discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube Neutrino Observatory
motivation: IceCube turned a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice into a neutrino telescope and opened a new window on the high-energy universe. In 2013 the collaboration reported the first PeV neutrinos, 'Bert' and 'Ernie', found in Shigeru Yoshida's extremely-high-energy search, followed by a diffuse astrophysical flux well above the atmospheric background. Subsequent work identified the blazar TXS 0506+056 in coincidence with a flare, the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 as a steady source, and neutrino emission from the Galactic plane. Francis Halzen conceived and championed the project for decades; Albrecht Karle led the design, construction and operation of the detector. This is exactly the kind of patient, large-scale experiment that makes basic discoveries: after Kamiokande observed neutrinos from SN1987A, IceCube established neutrino astronomy at energies a million times higher, answering long-standing questions on cosmic-ray origins and complementing gravitational-wave and gamma-ray observations in multimessenger astronomy.
